The Clouds. Aristophanes' vicious satire of intellectualism, performed in 423 BCE, featuring Socrates as the central target. It's a comedy that launches a direct attack on a living, prominent philosopher—a freedom Athenian law allowed in theatre, though perhaps it came with consequences.

An elderly farmer named Strepsiades is drowning in debt. He hears that Socrates runs a "thought-shop" where men learn to win arguments through rhetorical tricks, and he decides to enroll. If he can master sophistic rhetoric, he can cheat his creditors legally.

Socrates is presented as absurd. He's suspended in a basket, studying clouds. He measures the jump distance of fleas. He's obsessed with abstract questions that have no bearing on practical life. The Chorus of Clouds represents shifting, insubstantial ideas—the flickering thoughts that the sophists teach students to manipulate. Right Reason and Wrong Reason are presented as equally valid debating techniques. Truth is irrelevant; winning the argument is everything.

Strepsiades brings his son Pheidippides to be trained. The boy learns the rhetorical tricks so well that he uses them against his own father—he beats him and then argues philosophically that beating your father is actually justified. Strepsiades is horrified. The very education meant to save him destroys his household.

The play savagely mocks the sophists, the traveling teachers who claimed to sell rhetorical skill for a fee. Aristophanes groups Socrates with them, though the historical Socrates actually opposed the sophists' moral relativism. No matter—the comedy serves its purpose. It reflects real anxiety in Athens about the decay of traditional values and the power of words divorced from moral truth.

This play would later become infamous as a precursor to Socrates' trial and execution in 399 BCE. Aristophanes had wielded theatre as a weapon, and history suggests it landed harder than comedy usually does.
